author: Catie Lightfoot
title: Michigan State University study links jail time to increased suicide risk - NewsBreak
text:
By Catie Lightfoot ,
3 hours ago
GRAND RAPIDS, Mich. (WOOD) — Researchers say one in five adults who die by suicide have spent at least one night in jail in the year prior.
A new study conducted by Michigan State University and Brown University is looking to save lives by offering support to those people recently released from jail.
The study found that a single session of safety planning and follow-up calls reduces suicide risk in the community by half.
Pine Rest opening pediatric center in Gaines Township Jennifer Johnson is an Endowed Professor of Public Health at Michigan State University. She said the idea for the study began in 2014, when the National Institute of Health discovered that many people at risk for suicide were interacting within the legal system.
“That’s the place where the people have the most life chaos going on there,” she said. “They’re only in for a few days. They’re coming in, they’re coming out.”
The federally funded study focused on 800 people in the Genesee County Jail and the Rhode Island Department of Corrections.
“This isn’t necessarily people who are going away for life, these aren’t necessarily hardened psychopaths, the jails just pick up a lot of folks who are in a rough patch,” Johnson said. “And so by doing this, what we’re trying to do is prevent community suicide.”
Participants received a brief safety planning intervention with follow-up support after their release.
“That’s been found to be really effective in emergency departments,” Johnson said. “But never, nothing had ever actually been tested among populations interacting with jails and police. So half of them received safety planning intervention, half got resources.”
LGBTQ young adults have higher rates of suicide risk. Why? Afterwards, participants were tracked for a year after their release. Johnson said the intervention led to a 55% reduction in suicide attempts and a 42% decrease in suicide-related events.
“And that’s a big deal, because like I said, if one in five U.S. suicides occurs in this year in the community, and we can reduce suicide attempts by more than half during that time period, that’s potentially more than 10% of all suicides that we could prevent,” she said.
Now, Johnson is applying for funding to set up a data base in Michigan for at-risk people recently released from jail and to connect them with local health systems.
